title: The Machine That Learned to Bowl
notes: One vertical film (9:16 reels, 4:5 LinkedIn). Each line is voiced separately with its own emotion. exag = Chatterbox exaggeration (0.25 flat .. 1.0 intense), cfg = pacing (lower = slower, more deliberate), pause = silence after the line in seconds.

lines.text: This ball was bowled by something that has never watched cricket.
No coach. No highlights. Nobody ever told it what a yorker is.
It found one anyway.
So how do you teach a machine to bowl?
First, it has to see. Not with eyes. With numbers.
Who's batting. How confident they look. What it bowled last ball, and the ball before that.
Eighteen numbers go in.
Four come out. Speed. Length. Line. Swing.
In between sits a tiny brain. One thousand, one hundred and fifty six numbers, called weights.
Change the weights, and you get a different bowler.
So which weights make a great one?
Honestly? I had no idea.
So I made a hundred and ninety two completely random brains, and threw them the ball.
It was carnage. Half volleys. Long hops. Twelve runs an over.
But a few of them, by pure luck, were slightly less terrible.
Those became parents. Their children got copies of their brains, with tiny random changes.
Most were worse. Some were better. Keep the best. Repeat.
Fifteen hundred generations later, my bowler was unplayable.
Bouncer. Yorker. Bouncer. Yorker. Hundred and fifteen. Hundred and fifty.
Three bouncers. In one over. That's not even legal.
It hadn't learned to bowl. It had learned to cheat.
My batters only judged surprise by how extreme a ball was. So it bowled extremes. Forever.
So I changed the rules. Batters now read patterns. Two bouncers per over, like real cricket.
And I started again. From nothing.
Generation one. Twelve runs an over.
Generation fifty. Five and a half.
Two fifty. It finds the stumps.
Fifteen hundred. Almost nothing gets away.
And this time, it didn't find a trick. It found a plan.
Against the slogger? Yorkers. Full and straight, right at the stumps.
Against the technician? Good length, outside off. Again, and again, and again. Until he edges one.
Against the tail ender? Zero bouncers. My expert plan used two. It knew better.
I wrote a plan for each batter myself. It beat all three.
A hundred and ninety two random brains. Fifteen hundred generations. Eighty three million deliveries.
Nobody taught it to bowl.
It learned.
